questions.question: Write the word equation for the complete burning of methane. Use the atoms in the molecules to explain how the atoms are rearranged, and show that the number of each kind of atom is the same before and after.
questions.expected_answer: Methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. One methane molecule (1 C, 4 H) reacts with two oxygen molecules (each 2 O, so 4 O). Bonds in methane and oxygen break; the carbon atom bonds with two oxygen atoms to form one carbon dioxide molecule, and the four hydrogen atoms bond with the other two oxygen atoms to form two water molecules (each H₂O). Before: 1 C, 4 H, 4 O. After: 1 C (in CO₂), 4 H (in 2 H₂O), 4 O (2 in CO₂ + 2 in 2 H₂O). The atoms are only rearranged.

questions.question: Explain the roles of bond breaking and bond forming in a chemical reaction, and use them to explain why burning methane is exothermic and why a spark is needed to start it.
questions.expected_answer: Breaking bonds requires energy, because bonded atoms attract each other; forming bonds releases energy. In burning methane, the energy released when the new bonds in carbon dioxide and water form is greater than the energy needed to break the bonds in methane and oxygen, so overall energy is released as heat and light: the reaction is exothermic. However, some bonds must break before any new ones form; at room temperature collisions are not energetic enough, so a spark or match supplies this starting (activation) energy. Once started, the energy released keeps the reaction going.

questions.question: List four signs of a chemical reaction. State the law of conservation of mass and describe an experiment with vinegar and baking soda that tests it, explaining the results with and without a lid.
questions.expected_answer: Signs: a gas is given off (bubbles); a colour change; a temperature change; light or flame; a precipitate forms; a new smell. Law: in a chemical reaction the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants, because atoms are only rearranged. Experiment: place baking soda in a bottle with a small tube of vinegar inside, seal it and weigh it; tip it to mix, then weigh again. In the sealed bottle the mass is unchanged because the carbon dioxide produced is trapped. With the lid off, the mass decreases because carbon dioxide escapes into the air; the mass is not destroyed, it leaves the balance.
